record.original_question: Give an elementary proof that there are infinitely many primes p such that neither p-2 nor p+2 is prime; in other words, prove by elementary means that infinitely many primes are not twin primes.

evidence.quote: How do you show there are infinitely many primes which are not twin primes. Trivial proof: There are infinitely many primes of the form 15k + 7 by Dirichlet, and not prime if add or subtract 2. But Dirichlet isn’t elementary!

artifact.self_contained_problem: A prime number $p$ is called isolated (or non-twin) if neither $p-2$ nor $p+2$ is prime. Give an elementary proof (i.e., one that does not invoke Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, the prime number theorem, Brun's sieve, or other non-elementary analytic machinery) that there exist infinitely many isolated primes.
artifact.status_search_result: Standard non-elementary arguments (Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions such as 15k+7, or Brun's theorem showing almost all primes are isolated) easily yield the result, but these are not elementary. A web search did not reveal an authoritative source confirming or denying the existence of a fully elementary proof of the infinitude of isolated primes; the problem of finding one appears not to be widely cataloged as solved.

status_evidence.title: Twin prime - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It follows from Brun's theorem that almost all primes are isolated in the sense that the ratio of the number of isolated primes less than n and the number of all primes less than n tends to 1.
status_evidence.claim: The infinitude of isolated primes is known via Brun's theorem, which is not elementary.
